events.title: Born to Seth
events.summary: Seth fathers Enosh at 105. Genesis adds that in Enosh's time people began to call on the name of the LORD.

events.title: Fathers Kenan and dies at 905
events.summary: At 90 he fathers Kenan. He lives 905 years and dies.

summary: Enosh is Seth's son and Adam's grandson. His name is an ordinary Hebrew word for 'human being', often with a sense of weakness or mortality. Genesis ties his lifetime to a new beginning: 'then began men to call upon the name of the LORD'.
textSays: Seth fathered Enosh at 105. In his days people began to call on the LORD's name. He fathered Kenan at 90 and died at 905. He appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles and Luke.

interpretations.view: The note about calling on the LORD marks the start of public worship among Seth's line, set against the violence of Cain's line in Genesis 4.
Some rabbis read the Hebrew verb as 'profaned' rather than 'began', so that Enosh's generation started idolatry by giving God's name to created things. The Hebrew allows both readings.

voice: Quiet and reverent, a man who feels his own frailty and turns that into prayer.

names.meaning: possibly 'possession' or 'smith'; related to the name Cain

events.title: Fathers Mahalalel and dies at 910
events.summary: Born to Enosh, he fathers Mahalalel at 70 and lives 910 years.

summary: Kenan is the fourth generation from Adam in Seth's line. Genesis records only his birth, his son and his age. His name sounds like Cain's, and several names in Seth's list echo names in Cain's list (Genesis 4), which scholars have long noticed.
textSays: Son of Enosh. He fathered Mahalalel at 70 and lived 910 years. Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes him as Cainan.

interpretations.view: The similar names in Genesis 4 and 5 (Kenan/Cain, Mahalalel/Mehujael, Jared/Irad, Enoch, Methuselah/Methushael, Lamech) suggest two versions of one ancient name list. This is widely discussed but debated.
They are two separate families. The similar names show the two lines living side by side, one marked by violence and one by worship.

voice: Plain and steady, a man known only for faithfully passing life on.

events.title: Fathers Jared and dies at 895
events.summary: Born to Kenan, he fathers Jared at 65 and lives 895 years.

summary: Mahalalel, whose name means 'praise of God', is Kenan's son and Jared's father. Genesis gives no story about him, only his place in the line from Adam to Noah.
textSays: Son of Kenan. He fathered Jared at 65 and lived 895 years. He appears in 1 Chronicles and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus.

interpretations.view: Some preachers read the meanings of the names from Adam to Noah as a hidden sentence about the gospel. This is a popular idea, not a scholarly one, and the meanings it relies on are often uncertain.

voice: Gentle and worshipful, as his name suggests.

events.title: Fathers Enoch
events.summary: At 162 he fathers Enoch, the man who 'walked with God'. Jared lives 962 years, the second-longest life recorded after Methuselah.

summary: Jared is Mahalalel's son and the father of Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. At 962 years his recorded life is second only to his grandson Methuselah's. His name means 'descent', which later Jewish writers connected with a story of angels coming down to earth.
textSays: Son of Mahalalel. He fathered Enoch at 162 and lived 962 years in all.

traditions.text: The Book of Watchers says rebel angels came down to earth in the days of Jared, linking his name ('descent') to their fall.
traditions.source: 1 Enoch 6.6 (Jewish apocalyptic text, c. 3rd century BC)

voice: An old, patient elder who has watched many generations come and go.

occupations: farmer (implied by his words about the ground)

events.title: Names his son Noah
events.summary: At 182 he fathers a son and names him Noah, saying this son will bring comfort from the hard toil of working the ground the LORD had cursed.

events.title: Dies at 777
events.summary: He lives 777 years. On the Hebrew numbers he dies about five years before the flood.

summary: This Lamech is Methuselah's son and Noah's father. He is a different man from Lamech of Cain's line, who boasted about revenge. This Lamech speaks only once, and his words are a hope: that his son will bring relief from the curse on the ground (Genesis 3:17). That hope connects Noah's story to the first promise of rescue.
textSays: Son of Methuselah. At 182 he fathered Noah and said, in effect, 'This one will comfort us in our work and the painful toil of our hands, because of the ground the LORD cursed.' He lived 777 years.

interpretations.view: His words show a family that remembered the curse of Genesis 3 and waited for God to answer it. Many see a faint line of hope running from Eve through Lamech to Noah.
The Greek Septuagint gives him 753 years and the Samaritan Pentateuch 653, so the ages in Genesis 5 vary between ancient versions.

traditions.text: When Noah is born with unusual brightness, Lamech fears the child was fathered by an angel, and his father Methuselah goes to Enoch for an answer.

voice: Weary from farming yet hopeful, a man who speaks of comfort and rest.

events.title: Born after the flood
events.summary: Shem fathers Arphaxad two years after the flood, when Shem is 100.

events.title: Fathers Shelah
events.summary: At 35 he fathers Shelah and lives another 403 years.

summary: Arphaxad is Shem's son, born two years after the flood. Through him the line of Shem runs on to Eber and, nine generations later, Abraham. Luke's genealogy places an extra name, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Shelah, following the Greek Old Testament.
textSays: Son of Shem, born two years after the flood. He fathered Shelah at 35 and lived 403 more years.

interpretations.view: The Hebrew text goes straight from Arphaxad to Shelah. The Greek Septuagint and Luke 3:36 have Arphaxad father Cainan, who then fathers Shelah. Scholars debate whether Cainan was added or dropped.
Some link the last part of his name to the Chaldeans (Hebrew Kasdim), but this is uncertain.

voice: A child of the new world after the flood, practical and forward-looking.

events.title: Fathers Eber
events.summary: At 30 he fathers Eber and lives another 403 years.

summary: Shelah is Arphaxad's son and Eber's father, a link in the chain from Shem to Abraham. He is not the same person as Shelah son of Judah (Genesis 38), who shares the name.
textSays: Son of Arphaxad. He fathered Eber at 30 and lived 403 more years. Luke calls him Sala.
voice: A man of few recorded words, remembered as a link in the family line.

names.meaning: the region beyond, the other side

events.title: Named as forefather of 'all the children of Eber'
events.summary: Genesis introduces Shem as 'the father of all the children of Eber', which signals that Eber's line matters.

events.title: Fathers Peleg and Joktan
events.summary: At 34 he fathers Peleg. His other son, Joktan, becomes the ancestor of Arabian tribes. Eber lives 464 years.

summary: Eber is Shelah's son and the father of Peleg and Joktan. Genesis singles him out: Shem is called 'the father of all the children of Eber'. Many readers connect his name with the word 'Hebrew', the name later given to Abraham (Genesis 14:13). The link is possible but not certain, because 'children of Eber' seems to cover more peoples than Israel alone.
textSays: Son of Shelah, father of Peleg and Joktan. He lived 464 years. Balaam's last oracle mentions ships that will 'afflict Eber' (Numbers 24:24).

interpretations.view: The Hebrews are named after Eber. Rabbinic stories picture Shem and Eber running a school where later patriarchs studied.
The word 'Hebrew' may come from a root meaning 'cross over', and some compare it with the 'Habiru', landless groups named in Bronze Age texts. The relationship is debated.

voice: A dignified elder, conscious that a people will bear his name.

events.title: 'In his days the earth was divided'
events.summary: Genesis explains his name: in his days the earth was divided. The text does not say what kind of division.

events.title: Fathers Reu
events.summary: At 30 he fathers Reu and lives another 209 years, 239 in all.

summary: Peleg is Eber's son. His name means 'division', and Genesis says it was given because in his days the earth was divided. Readers have long asked what this means. The most common answer links it to the scattering of peoples and languages at Babel, told in the next chapter.
textSays: Son of Eber and brother of Joktan. In his days the earth was divided. He fathered Reu at 30 and lived 239 years.

interpretations.view: The 'division' is the scattering of nations at the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1-9).
It refers to dividing land among clans, or to digging irrigation channels, since 'peleg' can mean a water channel (as in Psalm 1:3).
A few suggest it refers to continents splitting apart. Most scholars, including most conservative ones, do not accept this reading.

voice: Thoughtful, a man whose name reminds him that the human family has been broken apart.

events.title: Fathers Serug
events.summary: At 32 he fathers Serug and lives another 207 years.

summary: Reu is Peleg's son and Serug's father, the sixth generation after Shem. After Peleg, the recorded lifespans in Genesis 11 drop sharply, from over 400 years to around 230. Reu belongs to these shorter-lived generations.
textSays: Son of Peleg. He fathered Serug at 32 and lived 239 years in all. Luke calls him Ragau.

interpretations.view: Several names in this stretch (Serug, Nahor, Terah, Haran) match place names in northern Mesopotamia near Harran. Some suggest Reu's name may also preserve a regional name, but this is uncertain.

voice: Warm and companionable, as his name suggests.

events.title: Fathers Nahor
events.summary: At 30 he fathers Nahor and lives another 200 years.

summary: Serug is Reu's son and the great-grandfather of Abraham. A town called Sarugi near Harran in northern Mesopotamia is known from Assyrian records, and many scholars think the name of the family and the place are connected.
textSays: Son of Reu. He fathered Nahor at 30 and lived 230 years in all. Luke calls him Saruch.

interpretations.view: The name matches the town of Sarugi near Harran, which fits Genesis placing Abraham's family in that region.

traditions.text: The Book of Jubilees says that idol worship spread in Serug's day and that he was taught the ways of the Chaldeans.

voice: A man of the northern towns, rooted in the land his descendants would one day leave.

events.title: Fathers Terah
events.summary: At 29 he fathers Terah, Abraham's father, and lives another 119 years. His 148 years is the shortest recorded life in the list from Shem to Terah.

summary: Nahor son of Serug is Abraham's grandfather. He should not be confused with his grandson Nahor, Abraham's brother, whose family stayed near Harran and produced Rebekah, Laban, Leah and Rachel (Genesis 11:26-29; 24:15). Naming a grandson after a grandfather was a common custom, and the family name probably survives in the 'city of Nahor' (Genesis 24:10).
textSays: Son of Serug and father of Terah. He fathered Terah at 29 and lived 148 years in all. Joshua later reminds Israel that their ancestors, including Terah, 'served other gods' beyond the Euphrates.

interpretations.view: A town named Nahur near Harran appears in the Mari letters (18th century BC), which supports the idea that the family names reflect real places in northern Mesopotamia.

voice: A head of a Mesopotamian household, at home among the gods of his fathers.

names.meaning: possibly 'we will rebel' (folk etymology); origin debated

events.title: The first 'mighty one' on the earth
events.summary: Cush fathers Nimrod, who 'began to be a mighty one in the earth'. The Hebrew word (gibbor) means a warrior or strongman.

events.title: A mighty hunter before the LORD
events.summary: He becomes proverbial: people say 'Like Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD'.

events.title: Founds a kingdom in Shinar
events.summary: His kingdom begins with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar (southern Mesopotamia).

events.title: Builds in Assyria
events.summary: From there he (or, in the KJV reading, Asshur) goes into Assyria and builds Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah and Resen.

summary: Nimrod is a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham. Genesis calls him the first 'mighty one' on earth and a famous hunter, and credits him with founding the great cities of Babylonia and Assyria. He is the Bible's first picture of a king who builds an empire. Centuries later the prophet Micah calls Assyria 'the land of Nimrod'. Genesis never says he built the Tower of Babel, but later Jewish writers made that connection, and it became a popular tradition.
textSays: Son of Cush. A mighty one and a mighty hunter 'before the LORD'. His kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in Shinar, and he (or Asshur) built Nineveh and other Assyrian cities. Micah 5:6 uses 'the land of Nimrod' for Assyria.

interpretations.view: 'Before the LORD' means 'in defiance of the LORD'. Nimrod is the rebel who organised Babel and hunted men as well as animals.
'Before the LORD' is simply a superlative, meaning 'very great', and Genesis 10 is neutral about him.
He may reflect memories of an early Mesopotamian king or hero. Suggestions include Sargon of Akkad, Tukulti-Ninurta I, or the god Ninurta. None is certain.

strengths: Energy, strength and ability to organise
failures: Later tradition sees his empire-building as pride against God
turningPoints: Founding the first kingdom in Shinar

traditions.text: Nimrod persuaded people to build the tower at Babel as an act of defiance against God.

voice: Commanding and proud, a hunter-king who measures everything by strength and conquest.

events.title: Takes two wives
events.summary: He marries Adah and Zillah, the first marriage to more than one wife recorded in the Bible.

events.title: His sons found civilisation's crafts
events.summary: His sons Jabal, Jubal and Tubal-cain become the fathers of herding, music and metalwork. His daughter is Naamah.

events.title: The Song of Lamech
events.summary: He boasts to his wives that he killed a man for wounding him, and says that if Cain is avenged seven times, Lamech will be avenged seventy-seven times.

summary: This Lamech is a fifth-generation descendant of Cain, through Enoch (Cain's son), Irad, Mehujael and Methushael. He is not Noah's father. He marries two wives, fathers the founders of herding, music and metalwork, and sings a short poem bragging about killing a man. His song shows violence growing worse from Cain onward. Jesus' command to forgive 'seventy times seven' (Matthew 18:22) is often read as a deliberate reversal of Lamech's boast.
textSays: Descendant of Cain through Enoch, Irad, Mehujael and Methushael. He married Adah and Zillah. Adah bore Jabal and Jubal; Zillah bore Tubal-cain and Naamah. He boasted that he had killed a man for wounding him and claimed seventy-sevenfold vengeance.

interpretations.view: Lamech shows sin spreading and growing: from Cain's murder to boasting about killing. Jesus answers his 'seventy-seven times' revenge with 'seventy times seven' forgiveness.
Genesis 4 shows that culture and technology (cities, music, metal) grew in Cain's line. Skill and wickedness rise together; the text does not condemn the crafts themselves.

voice: Boastful and threatening, a man who sings about revenge.

events.title: Father of tent-dwellers and herders
events.summary: Born to Lamech and Adah, he is 'the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle'.

summary: Jabal is Lamech's son by Adah. Genesis names him as the father, meaning the founder, of people who live in tents and raise livestock. His full brother Jubal founded music, and his half-brother Tubal-cain founded metalworking.
textSays: Son of Lamech and Adah, brother of Jubal. He was the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock.

interpretations.view: Genesis 4 explains where the main ways of life came from: herding, music and metalwork. 'Father' here means founder or model, not literal ancestor of all herders.

voice: Practical and outdoors, a herdsman at home with tents and animals.

events.title: Forger of bronze and iron tools
events.summary: Born to Lamech and Zillah, he forges all kinds of tools from bronze and iron. His sister is Naamah.

summary: Tubal-cain is Lamech's son by Zillah. Genesis calls him the one who forged tools of bronze and iron. The second part of his name, 'cain', can mean 'smith', so his name may mean 'Tubal the smith'. He is the Bible's first metalworker.
textSays: Son of Lamech and Zillah, brother of Naamah, half-brother of Jabal and Jubal. He forged every kind of tool of bronze and iron.

interpretations.view: Some have compared his name with Vulcan, the Roman god of the forge. Most scholars think the likeness is coincidence.
Placed just before his father's violent song, his metalwork hints that new tools could become weapons.

voice: Strong, skilled and plain-spoken, a craftsman of the forge.

events.title: Becomes Abraham's wife
events.summary: Abraham takes Keturah as a wife. She bears Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah.

events.title: Her sons are sent east
events.summary: Abraham leaves everything to Isaac, gives gifts to his other sons and sends them away eastward.

summary: Keturah is Abraham's later wife, mentioned after Sarah's death. Her six sons become the ancestors of tribes in Arabia, including Midian, the people of Moses' father-in-law Jethro. Genesis calls her a wife, while 1 Chronicles calls her a concubine (a secondary wife). Genesis does not say exactly when the marriage began.
textSays: Abraham took Keturah as a wife. She bore six sons, including Midian. 1 Chronicles calls her Abraham's concubine. Abraham gave her sons gifts and sent them east, away from Isaac.

interpretations.view: She was a second wife or concubine, and her sons fulfil the promise that Abraham would be the father of many nations (Genesis 17:4).
Some rabbis identify Keturah with Hagar, saying Abraham brought Hagar back after Sarah died.

traditions.text: Keturah is Hagar under another name, called Keturah because her deeds were as pleasant as incense.

voice: Quiet and dignified, the mother of desert peoples.

events.title: Given to Rachel
events.summary: Laban gives Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maidservant at Rachel's wedding.

events.title: Bears Dan and Naphtali
events.summary: Childless Rachel gives Bilhah to Jacob so that she can have children 'through' her. Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali, and Rachel names them.

events.title: Reuben sleeps with her
events.summary: After Rachel dies, Jacob's eldest son Reuben sleeps with Bilhah. Jacob later strips Reuben of his firstborn rank for this (Genesis 49:3-4).

summary: Bilhah was Rachel's maidservant. When Rachel could not have children, she gave Bilhah to Jacob, following a custom known from ancient Near Eastern contracts in which a servant's child counted as the wife's. Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali, ancestors of two tribes. She had little say in what happened to her, and the text tells her story briefly.
textSays: Laban gave her to Rachel. Rachel gave her to Jacob as a wife, and she bore Dan and Naphtali. Reuben later slept with her, and Jacob heard of it.

interpretations.view: Marriage contracts from Nuzi and elsewhere let a childless wife provide a servant to bear children counted as hers, which explains Rachel's action.
Many note that Bilhah, like Hagar, is used for others' goals and never speaks, and read her story as a reminder of those with little power in the household.

voice: Silent in the text; imagined as patient and watchful, a servant who knows her place is not her own.

events.title: Given to Leah
events.summary: Laban gives Zilpah to Leah as her maidservant on Leah's wedding day.

events.title: Bears Gad and Asher
events.summary: When Leah stops having children she gives Zilpah to Jacob. Zilpah bears Gad and Asher, and Leah names them 'good fortune' and 'happy'.

summary: Zilpah was Leah's maidservant. In the rivalry between Leah and Rachel, Leah gave her to Jacob, and she bore Gad and Asher. Through them she became the mother of two of Israel's twelve tribes.
textSays: Laban gave her to Leah. Leah gave her to Jacob, and she bore Gad and Asher. Sixteen of Jacob's descendants who went to Egypt are counted through her.

interpretations.view: God builds Israel even through the messy rivalries of Jacob's household; the servant women's sons receive full shares among the tribes.

voice: Rarely heard; imagined as loyal to Leah and quietly proud of her sons.

events.title: Born to Leah
events.summary: Leah bears a daughter after her six sons and names her Dinah.

events.title: Taken by Shechem
events.summary: Dinah goes out to visit the women of the land. Shechem, son of the local ruler Hamor, takes her and lies with her by force, then says he loves her and wants to marry her.

events.title: Her brothers' deception and massacre
events.summary: Her brothers demand that the men of Shechem be circumcised. While they are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill all the men and take Dinah home. The other sons plunder the city.

events.title: Jacob's rebuke
events.summary: Jacob fears revenge from the neighbours. The brothers answer, 'Should he deal with our sister as with a harlot?' On his deathbed Jacob curses Simeon and Levi's anger.

events.title: Goes down to Egypt
events.summary: She is listed among Jacob's family who move to Egypt.

summary: Dinah is the only daughter of Jacob whose name is recorded. Her story in Genesis 34 is one of the hardest in the Bible. Shechem, a local prince, takes her by force and then asks to marry her. Her brothers Simeon and Levi trick the men of the city into being circumcised and then kill them all. Dinah herself never speaks, and the text leaves her feelings and later life untold. The chapter raises hard questions about violence against women, revenge, and how far Jacob's family had to go before it would reflect God's ways.
textSays: Daughter of Jacob and Leah. Shechem son of Hamor saw her, took her, lay with her and humbled her. He then sought to marry her. Simeon and Levi killed the men of the city and brought her out of Shechem's house. Jacob condemned their violence. She went down to Egypt with the family.

interpretations.view: The Hebrew words (took, lay with, humbled) describe rape. The brothers' anger is understandable, but their deceit and mass killing are condemned by Jacob in Genesis 49.
The vocabulary could describe sex without consent of her family rather than physical force. This minority reading is debated and criticised for softening the text.
Some rabbis blamed Dinah for 'going out'. Others reject this, and many modern Jewish and Christian readers see such blame as unjust to the victim.

traditions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15b; Targum on Job 2:9

voice: Silent in Genesis; imagined as a young woman whose story others told for her.

events.title: Born to Leah
events.summary: Leah names him Simeon because 'the LORD has heard that I was unloved'.

events.title: Massacre at Shechem
events.summary: With Levi he kills the men of Shechem to avenge their sister Dinah.

events.title: Held hostage by Joseph
events.summary: Joseph, still unrecognised, binds Simeon before his brothers' eyes and keeps him in Egypt until they return with Benjamin.

events.title: Jacob's deathbed words
events.summary: Jacob calls Simeon and Levi 'instruments of cruelty' and says they will be scattered in Israel.

events.title: A tribe scattered within Judah
events.summary: Simeon's tribe shrinks in the wilderness (from 59,300 to 22,200 fighting men) and receives towns inside Judah's territory, fulfilling Jacob's words.

summary: Simeon is Jacob and Leah's second son. With his brother Levi he took violent revenge on the city of Shechem after their sister Dinah was violated. Years later Joseph chose Simeon to keep as a hostage in Egypt, perhaps because of that violence or because he had a part in selling Joseph. Jacob's last words condemned Simeon's anger, and his tribe did shrink and lose a separate territory. Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 leaves Simeon out altogether.
textSays: Second son of Jacob and Leah. He and Levi killed the men of Shechem. Joseph bound him and kept him in Egypt. Jacob cursed his anger and said he would be scattered. His tribe received land inside Judah's inheritance.

interpretations.view: Joseph chose Simeon because he had been the one who threw Joseph into the pit or first proposed killing him.
Simeon and Levi show two outcomes of one curse: Levi's scattering became a priestly calling (Exodus 32:26-29), while Simeon's tribe faded into Judah.
The story may reflect the later history of a small tribe that was absorbed by Judah.

failures: Deceit and mass killing at Shechem

voice: Hot-tempered and blunt, quick to defend family honour and slow to count the cost.

events.title: Born after the mandrakes bargain
events.summary: Leah 'hires' a night with Jacob from Rachel in exchange for her son's mandrakes. She conceives and names the boy Issachar, 'reward'.

events.title: Jacob's blessing
events.summary: Jacob pictures Issachar as a strong donkey that sees good land and bends his shoulder to forced labour.

events.title: Men who understood the times
events.summary: Generations later the men of Issachar who join David are praised as 'men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do'.

summary: Issachar is Jacob and Leah's fifth son, born after a strange bargain between Leah and Rachel over mandrakes, a plant thought to help fertility. His name plays on the Hebrew word for 'hire' or 'reward'. His tribe settled in the fertile Jezreel Valley. Jacob's blessing pictures them as hardworking but willing to serve others for the sake of good land. Later, the men of Issachar were praised for wisdom about the times.
textSays: Fifth son of Jacob and Leah. Jacob compared him to a strong donkey who submits to labour. The tribe sent princes with Deborah (Judges 5:15), and its men understood the times (1 Chronicles 12:32).
voice: Steady and hardworking, a man who prefers a quiet field to a fight.

events.title: Leah's sixth son
events.summary: Leah names him Zebulun, hoping that now her husband will 'dwell with' or honour her.

events.title: Jacob's blessing
events.summary: Jacob says Zebulun will live by the seashore and be a haven for ships, with his border toward Sidon.

events.title: Risks their lives with Deborah
events.summary: Zebulun's men answer Barak's call and are praised in Deborah's song as a people who risked their lives to the death.

events.title: Galilee of the nations
events.summary: Isaiah promises that the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, once humbled, will see a great light. Matthew sees this fulfilled when Jesus settles in Capernaum.

summary: Zebulun is Jacob and Leah's sixth son. His tribe settled in lower Galilee, the hill country around Nazareth. Zebulun's warriors fought bravely with Deborah and Barak. Isaiah later promised that this northern region, the first to suffer Assyrian invasion, would see a great light. Matthew applies that promise to Jesus' ministry in Galilee.
textSays: Sixth son of Jacob and Leah. Jacob linked him with the sea and trade. His tribe fought under Barak and later sent 50,000 skilled soldiers to David (1 Chronicles 12:33). Isaiah and Matthew name his land as a place of coming light.
voice: Outgoing and adventurous, looking toward the sea routes and the wider world.

events.title: Born to Zilpah
events.summary: Leah's maidservant Zilpah bears him, and Leah says, 'Good fortune has come!'

events.title: Jacob's blessing
events.summary: In a play on his name, Jacob says raiders will raid Gad, but Gad will raid at their heels.

events.title: Settles east of the Jordan
events.summary: Gad's tribe, rich in livestock, asks for the grazing land of Gilead. Moses agrees on condition that they help conquer Canaan first.

events.title: The altar by the Jordan
events.summary: Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh build an altar by the Jordan. The other tribes nearly go to war until they learn it is a witness of shared faith, not a rival altar.

summary: Gad is Jacob's son by Zilpah, Leah's servant. His name means 'good fortune'. His tribe raised livestock and settled in Gilead, east of the Jordan, on the exposed frontier with Ammon and the desert peoples. Gadites became known as tough fighters, described as having 'faces like lions' (1 Chronicles 12:8).
textSays: Son of Jacob and Zilpah, full brother of Asher. Jacob foresaw Gad being attacked and striking back. His tribe received land east of the Jordan after promising to fight alongside the others.
voice: Brisk and battle-ready, a frontiersman used to defending his herds.

events.title: Born to Zilpah
events.summary: Leah calls him Asher: 'Happy am I, for women will call me blessed.'

events.title: Jacob's blessing
events.summary: Jacob promises Asher rich food fit for kings.

events.title: A tribe on the coast
events.summary: Asher fails to drive out the Canaanites of Acco and Sidon, and stays by the coast instead of joining Deborah's battle.

events.title: Anna of the tribe of Asher
events.summary: The prophetess Anna, who welcomes the infant Jesus in the temple, is from Asher.

summary: Asher is Jacob's second son by Zilpah. His name means 'happy'. His tribe received fertile land along the coast north of Mount Carmel, toward Tyre and Sidon, famous for olive oil. Asher did not drive out the coastal Canaanites and lived among them. Centuries later the elderly prophetess Anna, from Asher, was among the first to recognise the child Jesus.
textSays: Son of Jacob and Zilpah. Jacob and Moses blessed him with rich food and oil. His tribe lived among the Canaanites on the coast. Anna the prophetess was of his tribe.
voice: Cheerful and prosperous, fond of good food and good company.

events.title: Born to Bilhah
events.summary: Rachel names Bilhah's second son Naphtali: 'With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed.'

events.title: Jacob's blessing
events.summary: Jacob calls Naphtali a doe let loose who gives beautiful words.

events.title: Barak's tribe
events.summary: Barak, Deborah's general, comes from Kedesh in Naphtali, and Naphtali's men risk their lives in battle.

events.title: First into exile
events.summary: The Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser takes the land of Naphtali and deports its people.

events.title: A great light in Galilee
events.summary: Isaiah's promise of light to Zebulun and Naphtali is applied by Matthew to Jesus' ministry around the Sea of Galilee.

summary: Naphtali is Jacob's second son by Bilhah, Rachel's servant. Rachel named him after her 'wrestling' with her sister Leah. His tribe held the hills west of the Sea of Galilee. Barak came from Naphtali, and the tribe was among the first deported by Assyria. Jesus' Galilean ministry took place largely in this land, which Matthew links to Isaiah's promise of light.
textSays: Son of Jacob and Bilhah, brother of Dan. Jacob compared him to a free-running doe. His tribe settled in upper Galilee, fought with Barak, and was taken into exile by Assyria.
voice: Quick and graceful, with a way with words.

events.title: Born to Bilhah
events.summary: Rachel says, 'God has judged me and heard my voice,' and names Bilhah's son Dan.

events.title: Jacob's blessing
events.summary: Jacob says Dan will judge his people, but also calls him a snake by the road that bites the horse's heels.

events.title: The tribe moves north
events.summary: Pushed out of its coastal land, the tribe of Dan seizes the quiet town of Laish in the far north, renames it Dan, and sets up Micah's stolen idol there.

events.title: A golden calf at Dan
events.summary: Jeroboam I places one of his two golden calves at Dan, making it a centre of false worship.

summary: Dan is Jacob's first son by Bilhah, Rachel's servant. His name means 'judge'. The tribe first received land near the coast, where Samson the Danite later lived, but it was pushed into the hills and migrated to the far north. There it set up a stolen idol and later hosted one of Jeroboam's golden calves. 'From Dan to Beersheba' became a phrase for the whole land. Dan is left out of the list of tribes in Revelation 7, which has led to much speculation.
textSays: Son of Jacob and Bilhah. Jacob called him a judge and a snake by the road. His tribe moved north to Laish and worshipped Micah's idol there. Samson was a Danite (Judges 13:2).

interpretations.view: Dan's absence from Revelation 7 and Jacob's 'snake' image led some to say the Antichrist would come from Dan.
Dan is left out of Revelation 7 because of the tribe's early idolatry, or simply to keep the number at twelve once Joseph's sons are counted. The Antichrist idea is speculative.

voice: Shrewd and watchful, quick to strike when cornered.

nation: Israel (born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother)

events.title: Born in Egypt
events.summary: Joseph's second son by Asenath, born before the famine. Joseph names him Ephraim: 'God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.'

events.title: Adopted by Jacob
events.summary: Jacob claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, equal to Reuben and Simeon. This gives Joseph a double share among the tribes.

events.title: The crossed hands
events.summary: Jacob crosses his arms to put his right hand on the younger Ephraim. When Joseph objects, Jacob says the younger will be greater.

events.title: Grief and a new son
events.summary: Chronicles records that men of Gath killed some of Ephraim's sons. He mourns many days, then names a newborn son Beriah, 'in misfortune'.

events.title: Ancestor of Joshua
events.summary: Joshua son of Nun, Moses' successor, is from Ephraim's line.

summary: Ephraim is Joseph's younger son, born in Egypt to Joseph's Egyptian wife Asenath. Jacob adopted him and his brother Manasseh as his own sons, and in blessing them he deliberately put the younger Ephraim first. This pattern of the younger son being chosen runs right through Genesis (Isaac, Jacob, Joseph). Ephraim's tribe became the most powerful in the north. It produced Joshua, held the sanctuary at Shiloh, and its name became a poetic name for the whole northern kingdom of Israel, as in Hosea's 'How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?'
textSays: Second son of Joseph and Asenath, born in Egypt. Jacob adopted him and blessed him above his older brother. Joseph lived to see Ephraim's children 'of the third generation' (Genesis 50:23). His tribe was large and proud, and the prophets used 'Ephraim' for the northern kingdom.

interpretations.view: The crossed hands show that God's choice does not follow human rank or birth order. Some see the half-Egyptian Ephraim as an early sign of God's blessing reaching the nations.
To this day parents bless sons on the Sabbath with Jacob's words: 'God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh' (Genesis 48:20).
The story explains why the tribe of Ephraim came to dominate the north, and the later rivalry between Ephraim and Judah.

voice: Confident and favoured, aware that he received a blessing he did not earn by birth.

nation: Israel (born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother)

events.title: Joseph's firstborn
events.summary: Joseph names him Manasseh: 'God has made me forget all my toil and all my father's house.'

events.title: Blessed second
events.summary: Although he is the firstborn, Jacob puts his right hand on Ephraim and his left on Manasseh, saying both will be great but the younger greater.

events.title: Grandchildren on Joseph's knees
events.summary: Joseph lives to see the children of Manasseh's son Machir, who are 'brought up upon Joseph's knees'.

events.title: A tribe on both sides of the Jordan
events.summary: Half the tribe settles in Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan; the other half settles west of the Jordan around Shechem.

summary: Manasseh is Joseph's firstborn son, born in Egypt to Asenath. His name expresses Joseph's relief that God had helped him 'forget' his suffering. Jacob adopted him along with Ephraim but gave Ephraim the greater blessing. Manasseh's descendants became a large tribe split across both sides of the Jordan. Gideon came from Manasseh, as did the daughters of Zelophehad, who won inheritance rights for women.
textSays: Firstborn of Joseph and Asenath. Adopted by Jacob and blessed second. His son was Machir, father of Gilead. His tribe was divided east and west of the Jordan. 1 Chronicles 7:14 mentions an Aramean concubine as a mother in his household.

interpretations.view: Ephraim and Manasseh are held up as brothers without rivalry, in contrast to Cain and Abel or Jacob and Esau, which is why parents bless children in their names.
He is often used as an example of accepting God's choice of another without bitterness.

voice: Even-tempered and gracious, a firstborn content to share the blessing.

events.title: Buys Joseph
events.summary: The Midianite or Ishmaelite traders sell Joseph to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.

events.title: Puts Joseph in charge
events.summary: Seeing that the LORD makes everything Joseph does succeed, Potiphar puts him over his whole household. God blesses the household for Joseph's sake.

events.title: Jails Joseph
events.summary: Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce Joseph. When he refuses, she accuses him of attempted rape. Potiphar, angry, puts Joseph in the king's prison.

summary: Potiphar was an Egyptian official, called 'captain of the guard', who bought Joseph as a slave. He trusted Joseph with his whole household because he saw that God was with him. After his wife falsely accused Joseph, Potiphar had him imprisoned. Some readers notice that he sent Joseph to prison rather than having him killed, which may hint that he doubted his wife's story. He is a different man from Potipherah, Asenath's father.
textSays: An officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. He bought Joseph, prospered because of him, put him over his house, and then imprisoned him after his wife's accusation. The Hebrew word for 'officer' (saris) can also mean 'eunuch'.

interpretations.view: A slave accused of attacking his master's wife would normally be executed, so the prison sentence suggests Potiphar was not fully convinced.
The text says only that he was angry. Putting Joseph in the royal prison may simply reflect his rank and access to that prison.

voice: Formal, busy and practical, a high official who trusts results.

names.meaning: Egyptian, probably 'belonging to the goddess Neith'

events.title: Given to Joseph as wife
events.summary: Pharaoh gives Joseph a new Egyptian name and marries him to Asenath, daughter of Potipherah, priest of On (Heliopolis).

events.title: Bears Manasseh and Ephraim
events.summary: Before the famine she bears Joseph two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.

summary: Asenath was an Egyptian woman, the daughter of a priest of the sun god at On (Heliopolis), whom Pharaoh gave to Joseph as his wife. She became the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim, and so of two of Israel's tribes. Genesis does not say whether she came to worship Israel's God. Later Jewish writers were troubled that a patriarch married a priest's daughter, and they told stories to explain it.
textSays: Daughter of Potipherah, priest of On. Pharaoh gave her to Joseph. She bore Manasseh and Ephraim in Egypt.

interpretations.view: Asenath was actually Dinah's daughter, carried to Egypt and raised by Potipherah, so Joseph did not marry outside the family.
Her marriage to Joseph is a picture of the church, drawn from the nations and joined to Christ.

traditions.text: In the novel *Joseph and Aseneth*, Aseneth rejects her idols, repents, and is transformed by an angel before marrying Joseph.
traditions.source: *Joseph and Aseneth* (Jewish or Christian romance, c. 1st century BC to 2nd century AD)

voice: Dignified and reserved, a priest's daughter between two worlds.

events.title: Born first by 'breaking out'
events.summary: Tamar bears twins. Zerah's hand comes out first and the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it, but Perez is born first. 'How hast thou broken forth?' she says, and he is named Perez.

events.title: Goes down to Egypt
events.summary: He and his sons Hezron and Hamul are listed among Jacob's family going to Egypt.

events.title: A blessing for Boaz's house
events.summary: The elders of Bethlehem bless Boaz: 'Let thy house be like the house of Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah.'

summary: Perez is the son of Judah and Tamar, born after Tamar disguised herself to secure the child Judah had wrongly denied her. He is a twin who 'broke through' ahead of his brother Zerah. Through Perez the line of Judah runs to Boaz, David and, in Matthew and Luke, to Jesus. His clan became the leading family of Judah.
textSays: Twin son of Judah and Tamar, born ahead of Zerah. Father of Hezron and Hamul. Named in the genealogies of Ruth, Chronicles, Matthew and Luke.

interpretations.view: Matthew names Tamar in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:3). Perez's birth from a scandalous situation shows God working his purposes through flawed people.
The Messiah is to come from Perez's line, through David; some rabbis call the Messiah 'son of Perez'.

voice: Bold and pushing forward, a firstborn by his own energy.

events.title: Goes down to Egypt
events.summary: He is listed among the grandsons of Judah who go to Egypt with Jacob.

events.title: Father of three clans
events.summary: His sons Jerahmeel, Ram and Chelubai (Caleb) head the major clans of Judah.

events.title: Marries into Manasseh
events.summary: At sixty he marries a daughter of Machir son of Manasseh. Their descendants include Jair, who held twenty-three towns in Gilead.

summary: Hezron is Perez's son and Judah's grandson, one of the family who went down to Egypt. In Chronicles he is the root of Judah's main clans: through Ram comes David's line, and through Chelubai (Caleb) comes the family of Hur and Bezalel. A late marriage to a daughter of Machir links Judah's family with the tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan.
textSays: Son of Perez. Father of Jerahmeel, Ram and Chelubai, and by a later marriage of Segub. Named in the genealogies of Ruth, Matthew and Luke.
voice: A patriarch of many clans, proud of his growing family.

events.title: Link in David's line
events.summary: Hezron fathers Ram, and Ram fathers Amminadab.

summary: Ram is Hezron's son and Amminadab's father. Nothing is told about him except his place in the line from Judah to David. He probably lived during Israel's years in Egypt. Some manuscripts of Luke have two different names (Admin and Arni) where the KJV has Aram.
textSays: Son of Hezron and father of Amminadab. Listed in Ruth, Chronicles and Matthew.
voice: A quiet link in a long chain, known only by his family.

events.title: His daughter marries Aaron
events.summary: Aaron marries Elisheba, Amminadab's daughter and Nahshon's sister. So the priestly line of Aaron and the royal line of Judah are joined by marriage.

events.title: Father of Nahshon
events.summary: His son Nahshon becomes the leader of Judah in the wilderness.

summary: Amminadab is Ram's son and Nahshon's father, in the line from Judah to David. He matters for another reason too: his daughter Elisheba married Aaron, so the mother of Israel's priests came from the family of Israel's future kings.
textSays: Father of Nahshon and of Elisheba, Aaron's wife. Listed in the genealogies of Ruth, Chronicles, Matthew and Luke.
voice: A respected elder of Judah who married his daughter into the priesthood.

roles: leader of the tribe of Judah

events.title: Chosen leader of Judah
events.summary: He is named head of Judah for the census and camps at the front, on the east side of the tabernacle.

events.title: First to bring an offering
events.summary: When the tabernacle is dedicated, Nahshon brings the first of the twelve tribal offerings.

events.title: Leads the march
events.summary: When Israel sets out from Sinai, Judah's division under Nahshon goes first.

summary: Nahshon son of Amminadab was the chief of Judah during the wilderness years. He led the first tribe in the camp and on the march, and brought the first offering at the tabernacle's dedication. His sister Elisheba was Aaron's wife. He stands in David's family line and in Jesus' genealogy.
textSays: Son of Amminadab, brother-in-law of Aaron, leader of Judah at Sinai. He brought the first dedication offering and led the march. Father of Salmon.

traditions.text: At the Red Sea, when the tribes hesitated, Nahshon was the first to walk into the water, and the sea parted only after it reached his neck.

voice: Decisive and dutiful, the kind of leader who steps out first.

events.title: Fathers Boaz by Rahab
events.summary: Matthew records that Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, the woman of Jericho who hid Israel's spies.

events.title: Link in David's line
events.summary: Nahshon fathers Salmon, and Salmon fathers Boaz.

summary: Salmon is Nahshon's son and Boaz's father. Only Matthew tells us his wife was Rahab, the Canaanite from Jericho who sheltered the spies. That means Boaz, who later married Ruth the Moabite, had a foreign mother himself. Matthew includes these women to show outsiders welcomed into Israel's royal line.
textSays: Son of Nahshon, husband of Rahab, father of Boaz. Chronicles spells his name Salma.

interpretations.view: Only four generations (Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse) span roughly 300 years from the conquest to David. Most scholars, conservative and critical, think the genealogy skips generations, as ancient genealogies often did. Others suggest very long lives.
Rabbinic tradition says Rahab married Joshua, not Salmon. Matthew's account differs from this.
Some suggest Salmon was one of the two spies Rahab hid, but the Bible does not say so.

voice: A man of Judah who married across a line others would not cross.

events.title: Ordered to kill Hebrew boys
events.summary: The king of Egypt commands Shiphrah and Puah to kill every Hebrew boy at birth.

events.title: Fears God and refuses
events.summary: Because they fear God, they let the boys live. When the king demands why, they say the Hebrew women give birth before a midwife arrives.

events.title: Rewarded by God
events.summary: God deals well with the midwives and gives them families of their own.

summary: Shiphrah and Puah were midwives who refused Pharaoh's order to kill newborn Hebrew boys. Their story is the first recorded act of civil disobedience in the Bible: they 'feared God' more than the king. Strikingly, Exodus names these two midwives but never names the Pharaoh. Their answer to the king was clever, and perhaps not fully true, but God blessed them.
textSays: One of two midwives commanded to kill Hebrew boys. She feared God and saved them, gave the king an explanation about Hebrew women giving birth quickly, and God gave her a household.

interpretations.view: Some say God rewarded their fear of him, not their deception. Others argue that misleading a murderous ruler is right when lives are at stake. Christians have cited them in debates about lying to protect the innocent.
The Hebrew can mean 'Hebrew midwives' or 'midwives to the Hebrews'. Josephus thought they were Egyptian. Their names are Semitic, which suggests Hebrews.

traditions.text: Shiphrah and Puah were Jochebed (Moses' mother) and Miriam under other names.

voice: Calm, quick-witted and unafraid of kings, because she fears God more.

events.title: Refuses Pharaoh's order
events.summary: With Shiphrah she disobeys the king's command to kill Hebrew boys at birth and explains herself cleverly when summoned.

events.title: Blessed with a household
events.summary: Because the midwives feared God, he made them houses (families).

summary: Puah was the second of the two midwives who defied Pharaoh's order to kill Hebrew baby boys. Her courage, with Shiphrah's, kept the boys of Israel alive in the generation of Moses. She should not be confused with Puah of Issachar (Judges 10:1), a man with a similar name.
textSays: One of two midwives who feared God, disobeyed the king, and were rewarded with households of their own.

traditions.text: Puah was Miriam, called Puah because she cooed to the newborns.

voice: Gentle with babies and firm with tyrants.

skills.name: Cutting and setting stones; wood carving

gifts.name: Filled with the Spirit of God for craftsmanship

events.title: Called by name
events.summary: God tells Moses he has called Bezalel by name and filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding and knowledge in every craft.

events.title: Given a partner and helpers
events.summary: Oholiab of Dan is appointed to work with him, and other skilled workers are given wisdom.

events.title: Gift to teach
events.summary: Moses announces Bezalel's calling to the people and says God has put it in his heart to teach others.

events.title: Builds the ark and furnishings
events.summary: With the workers he makes the tabernacle, and personally makes the ark of the covenant with its gold cover and cherubim.

events.title: His bronze altar remembered
events.summary: Centuries later Solomon worships at the bronze altar 'that Bezaleel had made'.

summary: Bezalel son of Uri, grandson of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, was the master craftsman who built the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant. He is the first person named in the Bible as 'filled with the Spirit of God', and the gift was for art and craftsmanship: gold, stone, wood and design. God also gave him the ability to teach others. His story shows that skilled manual work and beauty can be a calling from God, not just preaching or leadership.
textSays: Son of Uri son of Hur, of Judah. Called by name and filled with God's Spirit for every kind of craft. Worked with Oholiab and led the craftsmen who built the tabernacle and its furniture, including the ark.

interpretations.view: Bezalel is the classic biblical example of the Spirit equipping artists and workers, often cited in discussions of faith and work.
The rabbis said Bezalel 'knew how to combine the letters by which heaven and earth were created', linking his building of the tabernacle to God's creation of the world (b. Berakhot 55a).
Scholars note many echoes between the building of the tabernacle and the creation account in Genesis 1, making Bezalel's work a small copy of God's.

voice: Absorbed, careful and joyful in his work, speaking of materials and measurements with reverence.

names.meaning: uncertain; possibly 'white linen' or from the Egyptian god Horus

events.title: Holds up Moses' hands
events.summary: During the battle with Amalek, Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' tired hands, one on each side, until sunset, and Israel wins.

events.title: Left in charge
events.summary: When Moses goes up the mountain he tells the elders that Aaron and Hur are with them to settle disputes.

summary: Hur was a leader who, with Aaron, held up Moses' arms during the battle against Amalek at Rephidim. Moses later left him with Aaron in charge of the people. The craftsman Bezalel is called 'son of Uri, son of Hur', and 1 Chronicles traces this Hur back to Judah through Hezron and Caleb. Most readers assume this is the same Hur, though the text never says so directly. Hur then drops out of the story, and he is not mentioned in the golden calf episode.
textSays: With Aaron he held up Moses' hands at Rephidim, and he was left with Aaron to judge cases while Moses was on Sinai. A Hur of Judah was the grandfather of Bezalel.

interpretations.view: Hur is a model for supporters who hold up leaders in prayer and practical help.
Some midrash says Hur was killed for resisting the making of the golden calf, which is why he disappears from the story. This is not in the text.

traditions.text: Hur was the husband of Miriam, Moses' sister.

voice: Loyal and steady, more comfortable supporting than leading.

events.title: Sees the God of Israel
events.summary: With Moses, Aaron, Abihu and seventy elders he goes up the mountain, sees the God of Israel, and eats and drinks in his presence.

events.title: Ordained as priest
events.summary: He is set apart with his father and brothers to serve as priest.

events.title: Strange fire and death
events.summary: On the day the priesthood begins, Nadab and Abihu offer 'strange fire' which God had not commanded. Fire comes from the LORD and kills them.

summary: Nadab was Aaron's eldest son and was ordained as a priest. He was one of the few who went up Mount Sinai and saw God. Yet on the first day of his priestly service he and his brother Abihu offered 'strange fire', incense or fire God had not commanded, and fire from the LORD killed them. Moses explained it with God's words: 'I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me.' He died without children.
textSays: Eldest son of Aaron and Elisheba. Saw God on Sinai, was ordained priest, offered unauthorised fire with Abihu, and died before the LORD with no sons.

interpretations.view: Rabbis suggested several faults: they were drunk (the ban on priests drinking follows in Leviticus 10:9), they acted without consulting Moses, or they were impatient to take over leadership.
The story teaches that worship must be on God's terms, and that closeness to God brings greater responsibility.
What made the fire 'strange' is unclear: wrong source of coals, wrong time, wrong incense or wrong place. The text focuses on the fact that God had not commanded it.

voice: Eager and privileged, perhaps too sure of his own access to God.

events.title: Sees the God of Israel
events.summary: He is among those who see God on Sinai and eat and drink before him.

events.title: Strange fire and death
events.summary: With Nadab he offers unauthorised fire before the LORD and is struck dead.

events.title: Aaron told not to mourn
events.summary: Their cousins carry the bodies out. Aaron 'held his peace', and he and his remaining sons are told not to show public mourning while on duty.

summary: Abihu was Aaron's second son and a priest. With his older brother Nadab he saw God on Mount Sinai, and with Nadab he died on the first day of priestly service after offering fire God had not commanded. Their deaths left Eleazar and Ithamar to carry on Aaron's line. The story stands as a stark warning that being near God is serious.
textSays: Second son of Aaron. Saw God at Sinai, was ordained priest, offered unauthorised fire with Nadab, and died childless before the LORD.

interpretations.view: Interpreters read his death alongside Nadab's; see Nadab for the main views on what went wrong.

voice: Close to his brother in everything, bold in worship but careless of the boundaries.

events.title: Keeps the tabernacle accounts
events.summary: He supervises the Levites' record of materials used to build the tabernacle.

events.title: Rebuked and defended
events.summary: After his brothers' deaths, Moses is angry that Eleazar and Ithamar burned a sin offering instead of eating it. Aaron answers for them, and Moses accepts his reasoning.

events.title: Oversees the Gershonites and Merarites
events.summary: He directs the Levite clans that carry the tabernacle's curtains, frames and posts.

events.title: A priestly house
events.summary: In David's time the priests are divided into twenty-four groups: sixteen from Eleazar's line and eight from Ithamar's.

summary: Ithamar was Aaron's youngest son. After his older brothers Nadab and Abihu died, he and Eleazar carried on the priesthood. He was a capable administrator who kept the tabernacle accounts and supervised the Levites who carried it. His descendants formed one of the two priestly houses. Many interpreters believe Eli the priest of Shiloh came from his line.
textSays: Youngest son of Aaron. Ordained as priest, supervised the tabernacle records and two Levite clans, and founded one of the two branches of the priesthood (with Eleazar's).

interpretations.view: Eli's family descended from Ithamar, since Ahimelech and Abiathar (Eli's descendants) are counted among Ithamar's sons in 1 Chronicles 24:3. Josephus says the same. The Bible never states it in one place, so the link is an inference.

voice: Careful, orderly and humble, a man who keeps the lists straight.

events.title: Takes from the devoted things at Jericho
events.summary: Joshua warns that everything in Jericho is 'devoted' to the LORD: to be destroyed, or given to the LORD's treasury. Achan secretly takes some of it.

events.title: Defeat at Ai
events.summary: A small Israelite force is routed at Ai and thirty-six men die. The people's courage melts.

events.title: Found out by lot
events.summary: God tells Joshua that Israel has sinned. By casting lots, tribe by tribe and family by family, Achan is identified.

events.title: Confession
events.summary: Achan admits he saw a fine robe from Babylonia, 200 shekels of silver and a gold bar, 'coveted them, and took them', and buried them under his tent.

events.title: Stoned in the Valley of Achor
events.summary: The goods are found. Achan, his family, animals and possessions are taken to the Valley of Achor ('trouble'), stoned and burned, and a heap of stones is raised over them.

summary: Achan, from the tribe of Judah, secretly kept valuable plunder from Jericho that God had commanded to be devoted to him. Because of this, Israel lost its next battle at Ai. When he was identified by lot he confessed, and he and his household were executed in the Valley of Achor ('Valley of Trouble'). His story teaches that one person's hidden sin can harm the whole community. It is also one of the Bible's hardest passages, because his family died with him. Later the prophet Hosea promised that the Valley of Achor would become 'a door of hope'.
textSays: Son of Carmi, of Judah's clan of Zerah. He took a Babylonian robe, silver and gold from Jericho and hid them. Israel was defeated at Ai. He was found by lot, confessed, and was stoned with his family and possessions in the Valley of Achor. The story is recalled in Joshua 22:20 and 1 Chronicles 2:7.

interpretations.view: Israel is treated as one body: 'Israel hath sinned' (Joshua 7:11). The story shows how seriously God takes the holiness of the community at a founding moment, a theme later seen with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5).

Some think the family knew about the goods buried under the tent and shared the guilt. Others note that Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids punishing children for parents' sins and see this as a unique 'devoted thing' case, where contact made the whole household devoted. Still others find the passage morally troubling and read it as reflecting ancient views of collective guilt.
His confession follows a pattern often preached on: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid, echoing the sin in Eden (Genesis 3:6).

failures: Greed and concealment that cost thirty-six lives

voice: Defensive at first, then broken and frank: 'I saw, I coveted, I took.'

names.meaning: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah

gifts.name: Courage to bring a just case before Moses and God

events.title: Petition to Moses
events.summary: Their father Zelophehad has died with no sons. They stand before Moses, Eleazar and the leaders at the tabernacle and ask: why should our father's name vanish because he had no son? Give us land among his brothers.

events.title: God says they are right
events.summary: Moses brings their case before the LORD, who answers, 'The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.' A new law follows: if a man has no son, his inheritance passes to his daughter.

events.title: A condition added
events.summary: Leaders of their clan worry that the land will pass to another tribe if the daughters marry outside. Moses rules they may marry whom they wish within their father's tribe. They marry their cousins.

events.title: Claim their land
events.summary: In Canaan they remind Eleazar and Joshua of Moses' ruling and receive their inheritance among the men of Manasseh.

summary: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah were five sisters from the tribe of Manasseh. Their father died in the wilderness without sons, so under the usual custom his land would go to other men of the family. The sisters asked Moses publicly to give them their father's share. Moses took their case to God, who said they were right, and a new inheritance law was made for daughters. They followed up years later and received their land in Canaan. Their story is often cited as an example of women seeking justice within God's law, and of law developing to meet new cases.
textSays: Five daughters of Zelophehad son of Hepher, of Manasseh. They petitioned Moses, God approved their claim, and the law of inheritance was extended to daughters. They were asked to marry within their tribe, did so, and received land west of the Jordan.

interpretations.view: The rabbis praised them as wise, interpreters of the law, and righteous, and noted they waited for the right moment to speak (b. Bava Batra 119b).

They are often held up as models of faith-filled advocacy. Some stress that their goal was to preserve their father's name and land, not to overturn the family system; others stress that God sided with women's claims against custom.
The two chapters (Numbers 27 and 36) show how ancient Israelite law was expected to grow through real cases and divine rulings.

voice: Respectful but unafraid, speaking together with one clear argument.

events.title: Defeated at Edrei
events.summary: Og comes out with his army to fight Israel at Edrei. God tells Moses not to fear, and Israel defeats Og and takes his sixty fortified cities.

events.title: The giant's bed
events.summary: Og was the last of the Rephaim (a race of giants). His iron bed (or basalt coffin), nine cubits long, about four metres, was kept at Rabbah in Ammon.

events.title: Remembered in Israel's songs
events.summary: Psalms celebrate God's victory over Sihon and Og as part of how he gave Israel the land.

summary: Og was the Amorite king of Bashan, the fertile land east of the Sea of Galilee. He was the last of the Rephaim, a people remembered as giants, and his huge iron bed was a famous relic. Israel defeated him at Edrei just before entering Canaan, and his land went to half the tribe of Manasseh. Og and Sihon became a pair in Israel's memory, a reminder that God had already beaten the giants Israel once feared.
textSays: King of Bashan, last of the Rephaim. He attacked Israel at Edrei, was defeated and killed with all his people, and his sixty cities were taken. His bedstead was nine by four cubits.

interpretations.view: The 'bed of iron' may be a basalt sarcophagus or a ritual bed. Large dolmens (stone tombs) are common in the region of Bashan.

traditions.text: Og survived the flood by clinging to the ark and lived until Moses' day.
traditions.source: Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 61a; Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer 23

voice: Huge, proud and confident in his strength and fortresses.

events.title: Had taken land from Moab
events.summary: Before Israel arrived, Sihon had captured Moabite land up to the Arnon river and made Heshbon his capital.

events.title: Refuses Israel passage
events.summary: Moses asks peacefully to pass along the King's Highway without touching fields or wells. Sihon refuses and attacks at Jahaz.

events.title: Defeated
events.summary: Israel defeats Sihon and takes his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.

events.title: Recalled by Jephthah
events.summary: Generations later Jephthah tells the king of Ammon that Israel took this land from Sihon, not from Ammon.

summary: Sihon was the Amorite king of Heshbon, east of the Jordan. He had seized land from Moab. When Moses asked politely to pass through his territory, Sihon refused and attacked. Israel won, and his land became the home of Reuben and Gad. Deuteronomy says God 'hardened his spirit', echoing Pharaoh. Sihon's defeat, with Og's, became a key memory of God's faithfulness.
textSays: Amorite king at Heshbon who had taken Moabite land. He refused Israel passage, attacked, and was defeated, and Israel took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.

interpretations.view: Deuteronomy 2:30 says God hardened his spirit. As with Pharaoh, interpreters debate how this fits with Sihon's own choice to refuse peace.

voice: Suspicious and aggressive, a conqueror unwilling to let another people through.

events.title: Afraid of Israel
events.summary: Seeing what Israel did to the Amorites, Balak and Moab are terrified. 'This company shall lick up all that are round about us.'

events.title: Hires Balaam
events.summary: He sends rich gifts to the seer Balaam to come and curse Israel.

events.title: Three altars, three blessings
events.summary: Balak builds altars on three high places and offers sacrifices. Each time Balaam blesses Israel instead.

events.title: Sends Balaam away in anger
events.summary: Balak claps his hands in fury and dismisses Balaam, who pronounces a final oracle of a star coming out of Jacob.

events.title: Remembered as a warning
events.summary: Micah calls Israel to remember Balak's scheme. Revelation says Balaam taught Balak to lead Israel into idolatry and sexual sin.

summary: Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab when Israel camped on his border. Afraid to fight them, he tried to defeat them with words, hiring the famous seer Balaam to curse them. Again and again Balaam could only bless Israel, and Balak's plan collapsed. Later Scripture remembers Balak as one who tried to turn God's people against God, first by curse and then by temptation (Numbers 25 and Revelation 2:14).
textSays: King of Moab, son of Zippor. He hired Balaam to curse Israel, built altars on three high places, and was frustrated when Balaam blessed them instead. Joshua 24:9 says he 'warred against Israel'.

interpretations.view: Balak shows that no curse can overturn God's blessing (Numbers 23:8). Revelation uses him as a picture of seduction into compromise.
The weekly Torah portion bearing his name (Balak) is read as a lesson that God turns curses into blessings (Deuteronomy 23:5).

voice: Anxious, impatient and commanding, a king who thinks the right price can buy any outcome.

events.title: Oppresses Israel eighteen years
events.summary: Because Israel did evil, God strengthens Eglon. Allied with Ammon and Amalek, he takes the City of Palms (Jericho) and rules Israel for eighteen years.

events.title: Killed by Ehud
events.summary: Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, brings tribute, then claims a secret message from God. Alone in the king's cool upper room, he stabs Eglon, a very fat man, and escapes while the servants wait outside.

events.title: Moab defeated
events.summary: Ehud rallies Israel, they seize the Jordan fords, and ten thousand Moabites die. The land has rest eighty years.

summary: Eglon was a king of Moab who ruled over part of Israel for eighteen years, based at Jericho. Judges says God strengthened him because Israel had turned away. He was assassinated by the left-handed judge Ehud in one of the Bible's most vivid and darkly comic scenes, full of details about his size and his servants waiting outside the locked door.
textSays: King of Moab who, with Ammon and Amalek, took Jericho and dominated Israel for eighteen years. He was very fat. Ehud killed him in his upper room and Israel then defeated Moab.

interpretations.view: The story mocks the foreign oppressor. His name sounds like 'calf', and he is described like a fattened animal ready for slaughter.

voice: Comfortable, self-indulgent and easily flattered by a promised secret.

events.title: Kills six hundred Philistines
events.summary: With an ox goad, a long pointed stick for driving cattle, he kills six hundred Philistines and saves Israel.

events.title: Remembered in Deborah's song
events.summary: Deborah's song says that in the days of Shamgar the highways were deserted and travellers used back roads, because the land was so unsafe.

summary: Shamgar son of Anath is mentioned in one verse as a deliverer who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. He is not called a judge, and his name and his father's name (Anath was a Canaanite goddess) suggest he may not have been an Israelite. Deborah's song places him in a time when roads were unsafe. He shows God using an unlikely person and an ordinary farm tool.
textSays: Son of Anath. After Ehud, he killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and delivered Israel. Deborah's song mentions his days as a time of danger.

interpretations.view: 'Son of Anath' may mean he came from Beth-anath, or that he was a warrior devoted to the goddess Anath, or that he was a foreign mercenary. His Israelite identity is uncertain.
He is a model of using whatever is at hand for God's purposes.

voice: Terse and practical, a working man who fought with the tool in his hand.

nation: Canaanite (army of Jabin, king of Hazor)

events.title: Oppresses Israel twenty years
events.summary: As commander for Jabin king of Canaan, living at Harosheth-hagoyim, he oppresses Israel cruelly for twenty years with nine hundred iron chariots.

events.title: Routed at the Kishon
events.summary: He gathers his chariots against Barak at Mount Tabor. God throws his army into panic; Deborah's song says the stars fought and the river Kishon swept them away.

events.title: Flees to Jael's tent
events.summary: He runs on foot to the tent of Jael, whose clan is at peace with Jabin. She gives him milk, covers him, and while he sleeps drives a tent peg through his temple.

events.title: His mother waits
events.summary: Deborah's song pictures Sisera's mother at the window asking why his chariot is so slow, while her ladies imagine him dividing the spoil.

summary: Sisera was the commander of the Canaanite army of Jabin, king of Hazor, and oppressed northern Israel for twenty years with nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah and Barak led Israel against him at Mount Tabor. A sudden storm turned the river Kishon into a flood that trapped his chariots. Sisera fled on foot and was killed in his sleep by Jael. Deborah's song ends with a haunting picture of his mother waiting at the window for a son who will never come home.
textSays: Commander of Jabin's army, living at Harosheth-hagoyim. He oppressed Israel twenty years, was defeated by Barak, fled to Jael's tent and was killed by her with a tent peg. 1 Samuel 12:9 and Psalm 83:9 recall his defeat.

interpretations.view: His name is not Semitic, so some suggest he was of Sea Peoples (Philistine-related) or Hurrian background, serving as a mercenary commander.
The final scene with his mother humanises the enemy and shows the cost of war, while also mocking the expectation of plunder.
Ezra 2:53 lists 'children of Sisera' among temple servants after the exile. A Jewish tradition says descendants of Sisera later taught Torah, but the link to this Sisera is uncertain.

voice: Proud and commanding in his chariot, then exhausted and pleading when he begs for water.

names.meaning: worm; crimson (a dye made from a worm)

events.title: Saves Israel after Abimelech
events.summary: After Abimelech's violent reign, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, of Issachar, rises to save Israel. He lives at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, judges twenty-three years, and is buried there.

summary: Tola is one of the 'minor judges', whose stories are told in just a few lines. From the tribe of Issachar but living in Ephraim, he led Israel for twenty-three years after the chaos of Abimelech. His name and his father's name (Puah) match the names of Issachar's own sons in Genesis 46:13, a sign that clan names repeated across generations.
textSays: Son of Puah, son of Dodo, of Issachar. He arose to save Israel, lived at Shamir in Ephraim, judged twenty-three years, and was buried at Shamir.

interpretations.view: The minor judges (Tola, Jair, Ibzan, Elon, Abdon) are given in brief notes. Some scholars think they were local administrators rather than military deliverers, and that their terms may overlap.

voice: Steady and unassuming, a judge who brought quiet after violence.

events.title: Thirty sons on thirty donkeys
events.summary: Jair the Gileadite judges Israel twenty-two years. He has thirty sons who ride thirty donkeys and hold thirty towns, called Havvoth-jair ('villages of Jair'). He is buried at Kamon.

summary: Jair was a judge from Gilead, east of the Jordan, who led Israel for twenty-two years. His thirty sons riding thirty donkeys and governing thirty towns picture a wealthy, settled family; riding donkeys was a mark of status. The towns called 'villages of Jair' are linked to an earlier Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, in Numbers 32:41.
textSays: A Gileadite who judged Israel twenty-two years. He had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys and had thirty towns called Havvoth-jair. He was buried at Kamon.

interpretations.view: Some think the judge Jair was a descendant of the earlier Jair son of Manasseh (Numbers 32:41; 1 Chronicles 2:22) and inherited the 'villages of Jair'. Others think Judges reuses a famous clan name.
Some readers see the many sons and donkeys as a hint of growing dynasty-like power, a theme that becomes a problem later in Judges and Samuel.

voice: A prosperous patriarch of the frontier, proud of his sons and towns.

events.title: Marriages beyond the clan
events.summary: Ibzan of Bethlehem judges Israel seven years. He has thirty sons and thirty daughters; he sends his daughters to marry outside his clan and brings in thirty wives from outside for his sons.

summary: Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel for seven years after Jephthah. He is remembered for his large family and for arranging thirty marriages outward and thirty inward, which likely built alliances across clans. Scholars debate whether his Bethlehem is the town in Judah or a smaller Bethlehem in Zebulun.
textSays: Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel seven years. He had thirty sons and thirty daughters, arranged marriages outside his clan for all of them, and was buried at Bethlehem.

interpretations.view: Some place him in Bethlehem of Judah; many others think Bethlehem of Zebulun (Joshua 19:15) is more likely, since the minor judges around him are northern.

traditions.text: Ibzan was Boaz, the husband of Ruth.

voice: A shrewd family man who builds peace through marriages.

events.title: Judges ten years
events.summary: Elon the Zebulunite judges Israel ten years and is buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

summary: Elon from the tribe of Zebulun judged Israel for ten years. Judges records nothing else about him except his burial at Aijalon in Zebulun. Unlike the minor judges around him, no family details are given.
textSays: A Zebulunite who judged Israel ten years and was buried at Aijalon in Zebulun.
voice: Quiet and reliable, remembered only for faithful service.

events.title: Forty sons and thirty grandsons
events.summary: Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judges Israel eight years. He has forty sons and thirty grandsons who ride seventy donkeys. He is buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim.

summary: Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon in Ephraim, was the last of the minor judges before Samson. He judged for eight years, and his forty sons and thirty grandsons riding seventy donkeys show a wealthy and prominent family. Samuel's list of deliverers in 1 Samuel 12:11 includes a 'Bedan', whom some identify with Abdon.
textSays: Son of Hillel the Pirathonite. He judged Israel eight years, had forty sons and thirty grandsons on seventy donkeys, and was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim.

interpretations.view: The 'Bedan' of 1 Samuel 12:11 may be Abdon (the names are similar in Hebrew), or Barak (as in the Greek version), or an otherwise unknown judge.

voice: A wealthy elder of Ephraim, proud of his large household.

events.title: His wife meets an angel
events.summary: Manoah's wife is childless. The angel of the LORD tells her she will bear a son who must be a Nazirite from the womb and will begin to save Israel from the Philistines.

events.title: Prays for the visitor to return
events.summary: Manoah asks God to send the man again to teach them how to raise the boy. The angel returns, but only repeats what he told the wife.

events.title: Asks the angel's name
events.summary: Manoah offers a meal and asks the visitor's name. 'Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret (wonderful)?' The angel rises in the flame of the altar, and Manoah and his wife fall on their faces.

events.title: 'We shall surely die'
events.summary: Manoah panics that they have seen God. His wife reasons calmly that God would not have accepted their offering or told them all this if he meant to kill them.

events.title: Objects to a Philistine bride
events.summary: When grown Samson demands a Philistine wife from Timnah, Manoah and his wife protest, but go with him to arrange it. The text adds that this was 'of the LORD'.

events.title: Samson buried in his tomb
events.summary: After Samson's death his family bury him in Manoah's tomb between Zorah and Eshtaol.

summary: Manoah was a Danite from Zorah and the father of Samson. His wife, who is never named, received the angel's announcement of Samson's birth. Manoah's response is earnest but a little slow: he asks for more instructions, wants the visitor's name, and panics when he realises it was the angel of the LORD. His wife's calm good sense steadies him. Later he and his wife objected to Samson marrying a Philistine, but went along with it. The story contrasts sincere but anxious faith with quiet trust.
textSays: A man of Zorah of the clan of the Danites. His barren wife was told by the angel of the LORD she would bear Samson. Manoah prayed for further guidance, offered a sacrifice, saw the angel ascend in the flame, and feared death. He opposed Samson's marriage to a Philistine. Samson was buried in his tomb.

interpretations.view: The angel whose name is 'wonderful' (Hebrew pil'i) is read by many as an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ, linking to Isaiah 9:6 'Wonderful'. Others see a created angel speaking for God.
The narrator lets the unnamed wife be the more perceptive partner, a gentle reversal of expectations.
Some rabbis criticised Manoah for following behind his wife (Judges 13:11), while others defended him as respectful.

strengths: Desire to raise his son rightly
failures: Fearful and slow to grasp what God was doing
turningPoints: The angel's ascent in the flame

voice: Earnest, anxious and full of questions, a careful father who wants to get it right.

events.title: Steals and returns his mother's silver
events.summary: Micah confesses he took 1,100 pieces of silver his mother had cursed the thief over. She blesses him and has part of it made into a carved image and a cast idol.

events.title: Builds a shrine
events.summary: He sets up a house of gods with an ephod and household idols and makes a son his priest. 'In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.'

events.title: Hires a Levite
events.summary: A young Levite from Bethlehem arrives looking for work. Micah hires him as priest for ten pieces of silver a year, saying, 'Now know I that the LORD will do me good.'

events.title: Robbed by the Danites
events.summary: Six hundred Danite warriors heading north take his idols and his priest. When Micah chases them, they threaten him, and he goes home with nothing.

events.title: His idol set up at Dan
events.summary: The Danites set up Micah's image in their new city. The priest turns out to be Jonathan, a grandson of Moses, and his descendants serve there until the exile.

summary: Micah was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose story shows how confused Israel's religion became in the time of the judges.
