He stole silver from his mother, gave it back, and used it to make idols for a private shrine, all while using the LORD's name. He hired a wandering Levite as his family priest, thinking this guaranteed God's blessing. The tribe of Dan then stole both his idols and his priest and set them up in their new city. The narrator's repeated comment, 'every man did that which was right in his own eyes', is the key to the story.
textSays: A man of Ephraim who made a carved image and cast idol from his mother's silver, set up a shrine, hired a Levite as priest, and lost both to the Danites, who set up the idol at Dan. The priest was Jonathan son of Gershom.

interpretations.view: The story exposes religion made to suit oneself: mixing the LORD's name with idols and treating priests as hired help. It prepares for the need for a faithful king and for proper worship.
Judges 18:30 in the Hebrew writes 'Manasseh' with a raised letter n, and many scholars and rabbis think scribes added it to spare Moses' name from being linked to an idolatrous grandson.

voice: Pious-sounding but self-serving, confident that the right equipment and staff will make God bless him.

events.title: Son of a concubine
events.summary: Gideon, who refused to be king, has seventy sons by many wives, and one more by a concubine in Shechem, whom he names Abimelech, 'my father is king'.

events.title: Murders his seventy brothers
events.summary: With money from the temple of Baal-berith he hires reckless men and kills his brothers 'upon one stone'. Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes. The men of Shechem crown Abimelech king.

events.title: Jotham's fable
events.summary: From Mount Gerizim Jotham tells of trees seeking a king: only the useless bramble accepts. He prays that fire will come from Abimelech and Shechem and consume each other.

events.title: Destroys Shechem
events.summary: After three years God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem. A revolt under Gaal fails, and Abimelech razes the city, sows it with salt, and burns about a thousand people in the tower's stronghold.

events.title: Killed by a millstone
events.summary: Attacking the tower of Thebez, he is struck on the head by an upper millstone thrown by a woman. He orders his armour-bearer to kill him so no one will say a woman killed him.

summary: Abimelech was Gideon's son by a concubine from Shechem. Although Gideon refused to be king, Abimelech seized power by murdering seventy of his half-brothers and was crowned at Shechem, Israel's first attempt at kingship. His half-brother Jotham's fable of the bramble king predicted that Abimelech and Shechem would destroy each other, and they did. After three violent years he was killed by a millstone thrown by a woman at Thebez. Judges presents him as a warning about power taken by violence.
textSays: Son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) by a Shechemite concubine. He killed seventy brothers, was made king at Shechem, ruled three years, destroyed Shechem, and died at Thebez when a woman dropped a millstone on him. Judges says God repaid his wickedness.

interpretations.view: Abimelech is the anti-judge: chosen by no one but himself, saving no one, and killing his own people. His story shows what kingship looks like without God.
Many read Abimelech as the bitter fruit of Gideon's later choices: his many wives, his ephod (Judges 8:27), and naming a son 'my father is king'.

strengths: Ruthless energy and ability to win local backing

voice: Ambitious, smooth in persuasion and brutal in action; obsessed with his reputation to the last.

events.title: Marries into Elimelech's family
events.summary: She marries one of Naomi's sons. Ruth 4:10 shows Ruth married Mahlon, so Orpah's husband was Kilion.

events.title: Widowed
events.summary: After about ten years both of Naomi's sons die.

events.title: Kisses Naomi goodbye
events.summary: Setting out with Naomi, she is urged to go home and find a new husband. She weeps, kisses her mother-in-law and returns 'unto her people, and unto her gods', while Ruth clings to Naomi.

summary: Orpah was a Moabite woman who married Naomi's son Kilion. After both sons died, she started out for Judah with Naomi and Ruth. When Naomi urged them to go back, Orpah wept, kissed her goodbye and returned home. She did nothing wrong: she followed Naomi's own advice. Her sensible choice is the backdrop that makes Ruth's extraordinary loyalty stand out.
textSays: A Moabite who married one of Elimelech's sons (Kilion). After being widowed she went part of the way with Naomi, then at Naomi's urging kissed her and went back to her people and her gods.

interpretations.view: Orpah is not a villain. She obeys Naomi and acts reasonably. The book uses her to show that Ruth's choice was free and costly.
Some midrash links her name to 'back of the neck', since she turned her back on Naomi.

traditions.text: Orpah became the ancestor of Goliath and his brothers, the giants of Gath.

voice: Affectionate and tearful, torn between love for Naomi and the security of home.

alternatives.label: Earlier placement (if the genealogy is compressed)

events.title: Leaves Bethlehem in famine
events.summary: During a famine in the days of the judges, Elimelech, an Ephrathite of Bethlehem, takes his wife Naomi and sons Mahlon and Kilion to live in Moab.

events.title: Dies in Moab
events.summary: He dies there, leaving Naomi with her two sons.

events.title: His land redeemed by Boaz
events.summary: Back in Bethlehem, Naomi's need to sell Elimelech's field leads to Boaz buying it as kinsman-redeemer.

summary: Elimelech, whose name means 'my God is king', was a man of Bethlehem who moved his family to Moab during a famine. He died there, and his two sons died later, leaving Naomi alone. His name is ironic in a book set when 'there was no king in Israel'. Boaz was one of his relatives, and through Boaz's redemption of his land and his family name, Elimelech's line continued.
textSays: An Ephrathite from Bethlehem-judah, husband of Naomi and father of Mahlon and Kilion. He went to Moab in a famine and died there. Boaz was of his family, and redeemed his field.

interpretations.view: Some rabbis judged him harshly, saying he was a wealthy leader who abandoned his people in the famine, and that his and his sons' deaths were punishment.
The text does not blame him. Many think he simply did what families did in famine, as Abraham and Jacob had done before.

voice: A worried provider, making a hard choice to keep his family alive.

events.title: Marries a Moabite and dies
events.summary: He moves to Moab with his parents, marries there, and dies after about ten years without children.

events.title: His name preserved
events.summary: Boaz acquires Ruth, 'the wife of Mahlon', so that the dead man's name will not be cut off from his family and town.

summary: Mahlon was the elder son of Elimelech and Naomi and Ruth's first husband. He died in Moab without children. When Boaz married Ruth, he did it in part 'to raise up the name of the dead', so that Mahlon's family line would continue through Ruth's son.
textSays: Son of Elimelech and Naomi, husband of Ruth. He died in Moab. Boaz married Ruth to continue Mahlon's name.

interpretations.view: The names Mahlon and Kilion sound like 'sickness' and 'wasting away', which may be a storyteller's touch hinting at their early deaths. The meanings are not certain.

voice: Rarely heard; imagined as a gentle young man far from home.

events.title: Marries in Moab and dies
events.summary: He goes to Moab with his family, marries a Moabite woman, and dies there, leaving Naomi bereft of both sons.

events.title: His estate passes to Boaz
events.summary: Boaz buys from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Kilion and Mahlon.

summary: Kilion was the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi. He married Orpah in Moab and died there, childless. His death, with his brother's, left Naomi empty and set the scene for the book of Ruth.
textSays: Son of Elimelech and Naomi. Since Ruth was Mahlon's wife (Ruth 4:10), Orpah was Kilion's. He died in Moab; Boaz redeemed his share of the family property.
voice: Rarely heard; imagined as a young man who never made it home.
